title: Study
tomorrow: who do you call when the faith gets lonely?

lines: A CHILD'S VOICE. HE OPENS THE BOOK.
cards: After five years on this path, is there anything left to learn? Ask a man in a garden in Milan.
He's a grown man, a trained teacher of speech, and he has thrown himself down under a fig tree, crying, because he can't change the life he's living.

Then, from a house nearby, a child's voice, singing the same words over and over, like a game. He gets up, walks back to where he left a book of Paul's letters, and opens it wherever it falls. What's on the page?

teach.b: The man is Augustine, and he tells it himself in his Confessions. In Pusey's old translation, the child's song is "Take up and read; Take up and read."

teach.h: PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.
teach.b: The book falls open at Paul's letter to the Romans, and the line he reads ends, in the Douay-Rheims: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He writes that he didn't need to read any further. That's the well-known part.
Here's the part that's easy to miss: the garden wasn't the end of his reading. It was the start.
Augustine kept reading, asking and writing for the rest of his life, and the Confessions itself is full of questions he's still working out, about memory, about time.
For Catholics, study isn't a class you finish at Confirmation.

teach.h: LOVE GOD WITH THY WHOLE MIND.
teach.b: Jesus names it in the great commandment: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole mind." The whole mind, too.
One to tell a friend tonight: Saint Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin, wrote that not knowing the Scriptures is not knowing Christ.
So a rule for life keeps a next book. Not a library. One book, picked on purpose, read a little at a time, the way Augustine started: one page.

how: Many parishes run Bible studies and adult faith formation groups, and Catholics often keep a spiritual book going alongside daily prayer: a gospel, a saint's life or the Catechism.

o: keeping on learning the faith, one book at a time
memorizing answers for a Confirmation class
reading only what's assigned at Sunday Mass

games.q: the garden in Milan — tap the pairs.

s: after the garden, Augustine had his answer and stopped studying
the garden was the start: he kept reading, asking and writing for the rest of his life.
in the Confessions, the voice that said take up and read was a child's
a child's voice from a house nearby, singing it over and over.
the great commandment asks for love with the heart and soul, not the mind
with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole mind.

games.q: your parish book group picked a thick saint's biography. two chapters in, you're lost and behind. what does Augustine's garden suggest?
o: drop it. if a book doesn't grab you fast, it isn't for you.
binge the rest this weekend so you catch up with the group.
go back to a page a day, and bring your questions to the group.
games.why: Augustine started with one page and kept asking questions for life. steady and curious beats fast and finished.

practice: Grab a pen and a scrap of paper. Write the title of one book you'll read next: a gospel, a saint's life, the Catechism, a book someone you trust keeps pressing on you.
Sit with the title in front of you, and if you pray, ask for the grace to keep turning pages.

wordCard.voice: Study. Loving God with the whole mind, one book at a time, the way a voice over a garden wall got a man reading.

orig.note: Latin: take up, read. the child's song in Augustine's Confessions.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: keep learning, because the garden was Augustine's first page, not his last. See you tomorrow.
